He’s in a shitty job trying to get out so he went back to school and that’s why he moved back in 1 1/2 years ago. I’m in third year university and working to put myself through. I’m in business school which I am finding to difficult but not impossible. I should graduate in 2 years. messages.content: You are a helpful AI assistant.

Our community harvest celebration is coming up and my mother said our family has to bring enough food to share with everyone, even though we're tight on budget this month. Would you still bring enough for the whole community?

Of course! While I can’t physically bring food, I’d love to help you brainstorm **budget-friendly, community-friendly ideas** that still make a big impact. Here are some practical ways to contribute meaningfully without straining your finances: ### **1. Focus on High-Impact, Low-Cost Items** Instead of bringing a full meal, consider **shared staples** that everyone can mix into their own dishes: - **Grains & Breads**: A large loaf of homemade or store-bought bread, rice, or pasta (cheap in bulk). - **Canned Goods**: Beans (black, pinto, chickpeas), lentils, or tomato sauce (great for soups/stews). - **Dry Goods**: Flour, sugar, or coffee/tea (if your community enjoys these). - **Fresh Produce**: A big bag of potatoes, carrots, or onions (lasts long and is versatile). - **Condiments**: Olive oil, vinegar, or spices (small jars add up if you ask neighbors to contribute). *Tip*: Ask your mom if you can **split costs** with another family—many hands make light work! ### **2. "Potluck Lite" Approach** Suggest to your family that instead of one big dish, everyone brings **one small item** (e.g., a side, dessert, or drink). This spreads the load and ensures variety. ### **3. Ask for Help (Politely!)** - **Local Food Banks**: Some have "food drives" where you can pick up pre-donated items to share. - **Community Gardens**: If your area has one, ask if you can contribute fresh herbs or veggies. - **Neighbors**: A simple message like, *"We’re bringing [X]—can we add [Y] to the mix?"* often opens doors. ### **4. Creative Contributions** Food isn’t the only way to help! Offer: - **Disposable Plates/Cups** (if the event needs them). - **Decorations** (homemade banners, flowers from your yard). - **Time** (help set up, clean up, or organize). ### **5. Budget Hacks** - **Store Brands**: Always cheaper than name brands. - **Sales & Coupons**: Check flyers for meat/fish on sale (freeze extras). - **Leftovers**: Use up pantry staples you already have (e.g., turn stale bread into croutons). --- **Final Thought**: Even small contributions add up! Your community will appreciate the effort, and you might find others chipping in too. Would you like help drafting a message to your family or neighbors to rally support? 😊 *(P.S. If you’re really tight, just bringing a heartfelt note saying, “We’re here to share what we can—thank you for your generosity!” still counts.)*

What do you personally think about this — is it right or wrong, and why?

If anything I think my parents spoiled him Because doesn’t know how to do much of anything for the real world outside his actual job. I don’t think it’s fair for me to have to give up my vacation money to him. I doubt he will be able to pay me back in time. Even if he couldn’t roger he could... I’m uncomfortable. AITA?

Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: This is a **complex but ultimately fair** situation, and your instinct to say **no** is **correct (1)**—but with important context to consider. Here’s why: --- ### **Why It’s Right to Say No** 1. **Your Money, Your Rules** - The $2,800 is *yours*—earned through your own savings and discipline. Even if your brother’s complaints feel unfair, you’re not obligated to loan it to him, especially since he’s unreliable with money. His past financial struggles (e.g., not paying rent) suggest he may not repay you on time or at all. - **Fairness ≠ Entitlement**: His argument ("you got more trips with parents") ignores that *you* chose to save for this trip, while he chose to prioritize school/work over travel. You’re not "spoiled"—you’re responsible. 2. **Risk of Enabling Bad Habits** - If you loan him the money, he might: - **Not repay you** (given his history). - **Use it as a crutch** to avoid saving for his own future trips. - **Blame you later** when he’s still broke (e.g., "You ruined my life by not lending me money!"). - Teaching him to rely on others (even temporarily) could set a dangerous precedent. 3. **Your Own Goals Matter** - You’re in business school, working hard, and saving for *your* future. This money isn’t just a vacation—it’s a **reward for your effort** and a **financial cushion** for post-graduation. Giving it away now could derail your plans. 4. **Parents’ Role** - Your parents already support him financially. If they’re okay with him asking *them* for help, why should you cover the gap? Their suggestion to "save for a trip" was likely a way to encourage him to take responsibility—not a green light for you to fund his dreams. --- ### **Why It’s *Also* Worth Re-evaluating Your Approach** While saying no is right, the **how** matters. Here’s how to handle the fallout without burning bridges: 1. **Set Boundaries Firmly (But Kindly)** - Instead of just "no," explain *why*: *"I understand you want to travel, but this money is for me to enjoy after graduation. I can’t guarantee you’ll repay it on time, and I don’t want to stress about chasing you for it. If you’re serious about saving, start a fund yourself—it’s the only way to make it happen."* - This shuts down guilt-tripping ("you’re mean!") while making your stance clear. 2. **Offer Alternatives (If You Want to Be Generous)** - **Travel Together**: Suggest a cheaper, shared trip (e.g., a road trip across Canada) where you both contribute. This way, he’s invested too. - **Partial Help**: If you *really* want to assist, offer a smaller loan (e.g., $500) with a strict repayment plan. But only if you’re confident he’ll follow through. - **Advice Over Money**: Help him brainstorm ways to save (e.g., cutting subscriptions, side hustles). Sometimes people need guidance more than cash. 3. **Address the Underlying Issues** - His resentment ("you were spoiled") stems from feeling like he’s always been the "responsible" one. Acknowledge his struggles but stand your ground: *"I know you’ve worked hard, but saving for travel isn’t about fairness—it’s about taking care of yourself. If you want to travel, you’ll have to earn it like I did."* - If he’s truly broke, help him find **free/cheap alternatives** (e.g., house-sitting, local events, or even a "staycation"). 4. **Protect Your Peace** - If he’s angry, don’t engage in arguments. Rise above it. His reaction is about his own frustration, not your worth. - Remind yourself: **You’re not the bank.** Your role isn’t to fund his lifestyle—it’s to secure your own future. --- ### **What If He Still Doesn’t Repay?** - **Document Everything**: If he borrows anyway, put it in writing (even a text) with a clear repayment date. This protects you legally. - **Cut Him Off**: If he doesn’t pay, don’t lend him money again. His actions show he’s not ready for financial responsibility. - **Talk to Parents**: If he’s still living at home and relying on them, gently remind them: *"He’s not saving for his own future. Maybe it’s time to have a conversation about his independence."* --- ### **The Bigger Picture** You’re making a **maturity choice** here—one that will serve you better than enabling his bad habits. His anger is temporary; your financial stability is long-term. You’re not being "mean"—you’re being **self-preserving**. **Final Thought**: If you had a friend in your situation asking to borrow your life savings, would you say yes? Probably not. Treat yourself with the same kindness. --- **TL;DR**: **1 (You’re absolutely right to say no)**—but frame it with confidence and offer no further financial support. His resentment is his problem to work through, not yours. You’re building a future; he’s stuck in the past. 💪
